'Dr. Ride' takes its sweet time to rev up, but it goes the distance when the engine kicks in.
Dr. Ride’s American Beach House remains a sensitive work by an up-and-coming playwright.
American Beach House depicts a giant leap for both woman and womankind.
Birkenmeier creates very real characters and believable dialogue. However, she is weak on a dramatic event.
Birkenmeier struggles to create comprehensible histories for her characters.

There is a story of anguish wrought by repression, misguided choices, and systemic cultural homophobia and gender bias; however, “Dr. Ride’s American Beach House” does not rise to an epic tale of “queer anti-heroes” forging a pathway to self-acceptance and claiming true power and control.

cn.t: Birkenmeier's witty, weird play about women on a St. Louis rooftop in 1983 draws mostly positive notices for its distinctive dialogue and offbeat charm, though some critics find its languid pacing risks tedium.
